slides.background: Useful family words include père (father), mère (mother), frère (brother), sœur (sister), parents (parents) and grands-parents (grandparents).
slides.run: Spend about 3 minutes eliciting or revising the family words orally. Pupils point to each person in the visual, if available, and say who they are in French. The visual is not specified here, so do not expect a particular identification answer.

answers: mon père; ma mère; mes parents; mon frère; ma sœur; mes grands-parents
slides.misconceptions: Pupils may choose mon or ma according to their own gender, or use mes for one person. Explain that the French noun determines the choice: père and frère are masculine singular, mère and sœur are feminine singular, and parents and grands-parents are plural.
slides.background: French possessive adjectives agree with the noun that follows, not with the person who owns it. The noun’s grammatical gender is not always predictable from its meaning, so pupils learn each noun with its article or possessive.
slides.run: Allow about 4 minutes. Pupils match the words independently, then compare in pairs. Check the six combinations as a class and ask pupils to explain the singular or plural choice.

slides.misconceptions: “mes frère” uses the plural possessive with a singular noun. “ma frère” treats frère as feminine. Correct both by linking frère with masculine singular mon: mon frère.
slides.background: Mon can be used before a feminine singular noun beginning with a vowel sound, but that exception does not apply to frère.
slides.run: Give pupils about 2 minutes to choose independently, then ask them to justify their answer using the gender and number of frère.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may translate “he is twelve years old” word for word and use être. In French, age uses avoir: il a douze ans. They may also omit s’appelle or use the wrong subject pronoun; model the complete phrase, Mon frère s’appelle Hugo.
slides.background: French expresses age with avoir, literally “he has twelve years”. The adjective gentil is masculine singular here because it describes Hugo.
slides.run: Spend about 5 minutes reading the example aloud and checking its meaning. Pupils identify the name, age and trait, then practise saying the three details about an imaginary family member.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may write *il est treize ans; correct this to il a treize ans. They may use gentille for Louis; explain that gentil agrees with a masculine person. Remind pupils that the name phrase is il s’appelle Louis.
slides.background: Treize is the French word for 13. The adjective gentil has a feminine form, gentille, which adds an e.
slides.run: Allow about 6 minutes. Pupils write the three sentences independently, then check them in pairs for the correct phrase pattern and adjective ending. Take a few examples for class feedback.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may use the same adjective ending for both people. Explain that gentil describes a boy and gentille a girl; amusant describes a boy and amusante a girl. The final e marks the feminine form in these examples.
slides.background: Many French adjectives change form to agree with the person or thing they describe. These two adjectives add e in the feminine singular; pronunciation may not clearly reveal the spelling change.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils read each example aloud and compare the adjective endings. Ask them to say one sentence about each person in the pictures.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may keep un or une after a negative, or write *je n’ai pas de une sœur. After ne…pas, the indefinite article usually changes to de: je n’ai pas de sœur. The positive forms are j’ai un frère and j’ai une sœur.
slides.background: The negative expression is ne…pas around the verb: je n’ai pas. Before a noun, un or une generally becomes de after pas.
slides.run: Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils read the positive and negative examples, then explain what happens to un or une in the negative. Check understanding with an oral example about a sibling.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may use un instead of une with sœur, or keep un after pas in the negative. Reinforce the correct forms: une sœur in the positive and pas de frère in the negative.
slides.background: French uses de after pas in this construction, even when the noun is singular. The noun’s gender still determines the article in a positive sentence.
slides.run: Allow about 5 minutes. Pupils write both sentences independently and compare with a partner. Ask them to explain the change from un/une to de in the negative sentence.

slides.misconceptions: Pupils may use *elle est douze ans; correct the age with elle a douze ans. They may write amusant for Zoé; use amusante because the adjective describes a girl. They may also omit de after pas: je n’ai pas de frère.
slides.background: The five sentences combine the sibling patterns with the name, age and personality structures practised earlier. Amusante is the feminine singular form of amusant.
slides.run: Allow about 8 minutes for independent writing. Pupils then check in pairs that they have five sentences, with the correct negative phrase, age verb and feminine adjective. Review one sentence at a time as a class.

answers: Model answer: J’ai une sœur et je n’ai pas de frère. Ma sœur s’appelle Zoé. Elle a douze ans. Elle est amusante. (Answers will vary; accept a real or imaginary family and a suitable name, age and trait.)
slides.misconceptions: Pupils may mix up j’ai and je n’ai pas de, use être for age, or fail to agree a personality adjective with the family member. Correct with the patterns j’ai une sœur, je n’ai pas de frère, elle a douze ans and elle est amusante. For a boy, use amusant or gentil; for a girl, use amusante or gentille.
slides.background: A possessive such as ma in ma sœur agrees with the noun sœur. In the stretch sentence, pupils can reuse the same name, age and personality structures for a second relative, changing the pronoun and adjective ending as needed.
slides.run: Allow about 10 minutes. Pupils plan and write a short paragraph about a real or imaginary family. Ask them to include both a sibling they have and one they do not have, then details about one family member. Invite confident pupils to add the stretch detail and share their paragraph with a partner.
